name: NVIDIA NVLink 3.0
bandwidth_basis: PER LINK, UNIDIRECTIONAL. NVLink 3.0 defines a link as two 25 GB/s sub-links, one per direction, so a link is 50 GB/s bidirectional; the recorded value is the per-direction half. An A100 aggregates 12 such links = 300 GB/s per direction per GPU, which vendors quote as the 600 GB/s bidirectional total.
topology: Direct point-to-point links between GPU pairs. All-to-all full mesh is only practical up to 8 GPUs; beyond that, NVSwitch is required to avoid partial connectivity.
switching: None for direct-attached air-cooled parts. NVSwitch 3 provides an 8-GPU switched domain; without it an 8-GPU node is a partial mesh and the weakest link sets the all-reduce time for the whole group.
notes: AUDIT: status downgraded verified -> contested. This record's ONLY source is Wikipedia (link-wikipedia-nvlink, kind 'review'); the 600 GB/s aggregate and the 12x25 GB/s link structure should be re-checked against the A100 datasheet, which NVIDIA publishes first-party. Foundational scale-up fabric: one coherent low-latency domain, sub-microsecond-class latency, hardware-managed direct memory access between GPUs. Inference consequence: tensor-parallel sharding wants the highest per-direction fabric rate available, because every layer boundary ships activations across the link. The bidirectional aggregate figure that dominates marketing is not what a single collective move sees. On a partial mesh, an all-reduce that must route over a 2-hop path pays 2x the per-hop cost on that pair, so hierarchy-aware ring/tree algorithms beat flat ones. Cited figures come from a secondary source for the link-layer structure (a sub-link is 25 GB/s, a link is 50 GB/s) because NVIDIA's public pages quote only the per-GPU aggregate; the 600 GB/s A100 total is likewise from the secondary source.
